title: An order book with two heaps
objectives: Track the best bid and ask with two heaps.
Match crossed orders by price-time priority, with partial fills

screens.title: Who trades first
screens.prose: An order book holds buy orders (**bids**) and sell orders (**asks**) that have not traded yet. A buyer who wants to trade now takes the cheapest ask. A seller takes the highest bid.

state.caption: Bids below the spread, asks above

screens.question: Tap the level a buyer trades against first, and the level a seller trades against first.

hints.text: A buyer wants the lowest price on offer.
The asks are the prices on offer: £100.02, £100.03, £100.05.
The buyer takes £100.02; the seller takes the highest bid, £100.00.

feedback.correct: £100.02 for the buyer and £100.00 for the seller.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. A buyer takes the lowest ask, a seller the highest bid.

byKey.ask2: A buyer pays the ask price, so it wants the lowest ask, not the highest.
byKey.bid2: A seller receives the bid price, so it wants the highest bid, not the lowest.
byKey.bid1: £99.99 is lower than £100.00. A seller takes the highest bid first.

explain.text: The highest bid, £100.00, is the **best bid**; the lowest ask, £100.02, is the **best ask**. The book must know both after every order. That is a max-heap of bids and a min-heap of asks.

screens.title: A max-heap from heapq
screens.prose:
`heapq` is a min-heap, so bids are stored with the price negated. The time breaks ties.

```python
bids = []
heapq.heappush(bids, (-100.00, 1, "B1"))
heapq.heappush(bids, (-99.99, 2, "B2"))
heapq.heappush(bids, (-100.00, 3, "B3"))
```
screens.question: What is `bids[0]`?

options.why: You read −99.99 as smaller. It is larger than −100.00, so B2 is not on top.
B3 ties B1 on price but arrived later. The time, 1 against 3, puts B1 first.
The heap holds exactly what was pushed: the price stays negated until you read it out.

hints.text: The smallest stored tuple is on top.
−100.00 is smaller than −99.99.
B1 and B3 tie on −100.00; time 1 beats time 3.

feedback.correct: The highest price, and the earliest order at that price.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compare the stored tuples, negated prices first.

explain.text: Negating turns the highest price into the smallest stored value. The best bid is `-bids[0][0]`, £100.00, read in $O(1)$. Only the price is negated; the time stays as it is, so earlier still wins.

screens.title: Quotes after each message
screens.prose: Start from this book. Bids: B1 £100.00, B2 £99.99, B3 £99.98. Asks: A1 £100.02, A2 £100.03, A3 £100.05. Then four messages arrive, one after another.

state.caption: The book before the four messages

screens.question: Fill in the best bid and best ask after each message.

hints.text: Each message changes one side only. Carry the other side down unchanged.
A4 at £100.01 undercuts A1 at £100.02, so it becomes the best ask.

feedback.correct: Each add or cancel can move the top of one heap.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Apply the messages in order, one side at a time.

byKey.r0c2: A4 sells at £100.01, below A1's £100.02, so the best ask drops to £100.01.
byKey.r1c1: B1 at £100.00 is gone, so the next best bid is B2 at £99.99.
byKey.r3c2: With A4 cancelled, the lowest ask is A1 again, £100.02.

explain.text: A4 undercuts the asks; cancelling B1 exposes B2; B4 restores £100.00; cancelling A4 exposes A1. Every quote is the top of one heap after one push or one removal.

screens.title: An order that crosses
screens.prose: A buy order for 500 at £100.03 arrives. Its price meets the best ask, so it **matches**. It trades with A1 first, then A2, each at the resting order's own price, and partial fills are allowed.
screens.question: How many shares are left resting at £100.03 afterwards?

hints.text: Fill from the best ask upwards while the ask is no higher than £100.03.
200 trade at £100.02 with A1. 300 of the order remain.
Those 300 trade with A2, which had 400: 100 are left.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Take 200 at £100.02 first, then the rest at £100.03.

byKey.all: You left A2 untouched. After A1's 200, the order still needs 300, and A2 supplies them.
byKey.none: The order needs only 300 more after A1, and A2 holds 400.

explain.text: The order sweeps two levels: 200 at £100.02, then 300 at £100.03, for £50,013 in all. A2 keeps 100: a partial fill. The £100.05 ask is above the limit, so it is never touched.

screens.title: Same price, first come
screens.prose: Two sell orders rest at £100.02: A1 arrived at time 1 with 200 shares, A5 at time 5 with 300. A buy for 250 at £100.02 arrives. This is **price-time priority**: best price first, then earliest.
screens.question: How many shares does each sell order fill?

hints.text: Same price, so time decides who goes first.
A1 arrived first and fills completely: 200.
The buy has 50 left for A5.

feedback.correct: A1 fills 200 in full, A5 fills the last 50.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Fill the earlier order completely before the later one gets any.

byKey.r0c3: A1 was first at this price, so it fills completely: all 200.
byKey.r1c3: After A1's 200, only 50 of the 250 remain for A5.

explain.text: The earlier order at the best price trades first. A heap does this for free when the time sits second in the tuple: `(price, time, id)`.

screens.title: Cancelling from a heap
screens.prose: B2 is cancelled. Its entry `(-99.99, 2, "B2")` sits somewhere in the middle of the bid heap, not at the top.

state.caption: The bid heap as a list

screens.question: Which way keeps every operation correct and fast?

options.text: Add `"B2"` to a set of dead ids; drop dead entries when they reach the top

options.why: Removing from the middle shifts later items, breaking the parent and child positions. Finding the entry is $O(n)$ too.
That is correct but $O(n)$ per cancel. Most orders on a busy book are cancelled.

options.text: Set its quantity to 0 and leave it
options.why: Then `best_bid` can report a price nobody is bidding, unless every read skips it.

hints.text: A heap can only remove cheaply from the top.
Leave the entry where it is, but remember that it is dead.
When a dead entry reaches the top, pop it and look again: **lazy deletion**.

feedback.correct: Mark it now, remove it when it surfaces.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Which option avoids touching the middle of the heap?

byKey.b: You removed from the middle. The list stays a list, but the heap rule can break, and later pops come out wrong.

explain.text: Cancelling becomes $O(1)$: add the id to a set, or delete it from a dict of live orders. Reads drop dead entries off the top first. Each entry is popped at most once, so the clean-up is paid for once.

canvas.caption: B2 stays in the list but is skipped when it reaches the top

screens.title: A quote nobody is making
screens.prose:
This book uses lazy deletion: `cancel` adds the id to `self.cancelled`. Then `cancel("B1")` runs on a book whose bids are B1 at £100.00 and B2 at £99.99.

```python
def best_bid(self):
    if not self.bids:
        return None
    return -self.bids[0][0]
```

state.caption: B1 is cancelled but its entry is still in the heap

screens.question: What does this `best_bid()` return?

options.why: That is the true best bid, but this code never looks at `cancelled`. B1's entry is still on top.
The heap still holds both entries, so it is not empty.

hints.text: Does the code read `self.cancelled` anywhere?
The cancelled entry was never removed from `self.bids`.
It returns the top entry's price: B1's £100.00.

feedback.correct: It quotes a cancelled order's price.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Read the code as it is, not as it should be.

byKey.b: You expected lazy deletion to clean up by itself. It only works if every read drops dead entries from the top first.

explain.text: The book shows a £100.00 bid that nobody is making; a seller would expect a fill that cannot happen. The fix: `while self.bids and self.bids[0][2] in self.cancelled: heapq.heappop(self.bids)` before reading. `match` must skip dead entries the same way.

screens.title: What each operation costs
screens.prose:
With $n$ live entries:

$$\begin{aligned} \text{add: } & O(\log n) \\ \text{cancel: } & O(1) \\ \text{best: } & O(1) \text{ amortised} \\ \text{each fill: } & O(\log n) \end{aligned}$$

"Amortised" means averaged over all calls. A read may pop many dead entries, but each entry is pushed once and popped at most once.
screens.question: A day brings 1,000,000 adds and 900,000 cancels. At most how many dead entries can all the reads pop, in total?

feedback.correct: At most 900,000: each cancelled entry is popped once.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. How many times can one dead entry be popped?

byKey.adds: Only cancelled orders leave dead entries. Filled ones are removed as they trade.
byKey.product: A dead entry is popped once and then it is gone. It cannot be popped by every read.

explain.text: Each cancel creates one dead entry, and popping removes it for good. So all reads together pop at most 900,000, about one per cancel. Spread over the day, a read costs $O(1)$ plus that share.

screens.title: What real engines add
screens.prose: Our two heaps are the core of a matching engine. Real exchanges handle millions of messages a second and add more around that core.
screens.question: Select all that apply: which of these do real matching engines add?

options.text: Price levels in an array indexed by tick, each level a first-in, first-out queue
A dict from order id to its order, so a cancel finds it at once
Self-match prevention: two orders from the same firm must not trade
Re-sorting the whole book after every message
options.why: That costs $O(n \log n)$ per message. Heaps or arrays by tick keep the order as they go.

options.text: Filling a crossed order at the midpoint of the two prices
options.why: Fills happen at the resting order's price. That is part of the price-time rule.

hints.text: Three of these make the engine faster or safer.
Prices sit on a tick grid, so an array index replaces a heap search.
Arrays by tick, an id map, and self-match prevention. Re-sorting and midpoint fills are not used.

feedback.correct: Arrays by tick, an id map, and self-match prevention.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Keep what makes each message cheap or prevents a bad trade.

byKey.d: You picked re-sorting. That is $O(n \log n)$ per message; engines keep order incrementally.
byKey.e: You picked midpoint fills. The resting order's price is the rule.

explain.text: Prices sit on a tick grid, so an index finds a level in $O(1)$, with a queue for time priority. An id map makes cancels $O(1)$ without lazy deletion. Self-match prevention stops a firm trading with itself.

screens.title: The matching engine
screens.prose: Build the book. `side` is `"buy"` or `"sell"`. `add` only rests an order; `match` trades while the best bid is at least the best ask. Each fill is `(buy_id, sell_id, price, qty)`, at the price of whichever order arrived first. Partial fills leave the rest resting. An empty side quotes `None`; cancelling an unknown or finished id does nothing.

state.caption: Price-time priority; fills at the resting price

screens.question: Write the `OrderBook` class.

tests.call: (len(r[0]), sum(f[3] for f in r[0]), r[1], r[2])
tests.setup: evs = [('add', f'B{i}', 'buy', 1000 - i % 50, 10) for i in range(4000)] + [('add', f'S{i}', 'sell', 1001 + i % 50, 10) for i in range(4000)] + [('cancel', f'B{i}') for i in range(0, 4000, 3)] + [('add', 'BIG', 'buy', 1020, 15000), ('match',), ('best_bid',), ('best_ask',)]; r = play(evs)

widget.how: Check runs 12 hidden tests. `play(events)` runs a list of method calls on a new book and collects what `best_bid`, `best_ask` and `match` return. Test 12 has 8,000 orders.

hints.text: Keep `bids` as `(-price, time, id)`, `asks` as `(price, time, id)`, and a dict of live orders: id to `[side, price, qty, time]`.
Cancel deletes from the dict. A helper pops entries from the top of a heap while their id is not live.
`match`: while both tops exist and bid ≥ ask, trade `min` of the two quantities at the earlier order's price. Delete orders that reach 0.

feedback.correct: Price-time priority, lazy cancels and partial fills, all in two heaps.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Check the first failing test.

byKey.test-1: Test 1 is an empty book. Both quotes are `None` and `match` returns `[]`.
byKey.test-3: Test 3 cancels the best bid. Skip dead entries before reading the top.
byKey.test-5: Test 5 has two asks at one price. The earlier one, A1, must fill first.
byKey.test-6: Test 6: the buy rested first at £100.05, so the fill is at £100.05, not the seller's £100.00.
byKey.test-7: Test 7 cancels A1 before the buy arrives. `match` must skip dead entries too.

explain.text: In the fixed sequence of test 11, B3 sweeps A1 and A3 at £100.02 and part of A2 at £100.03. A4 then sells at £99.98 into B2 at £99.99, the resting price. Each step is a heap push, a pop or an $O(1)$ dict change.

canvas.caption: Two heaps, one dict: the core of a matching engine

ideas: Bids live in a max-heap (`(-price, time, id)` in `heapq`) and asks in a min-heap. Both best quotes sit at index 0.
Orders match while the best bid is at least the best ask. Best price goes first, then earliest on a tie, at the resting order's price, and partial fills are allowed.
Cancel by marking the order dead and dropping dead entries as they reach the top. Never delete from the middle of a heap.

explain.text: An empty side has no best quote, so `None`. `match` must check for it before comparing prices.

quiz.prose: Bids go into `heapq` as tuples. On equal prices the earliest order must come out first.
quiz.question: Which tuple does that?

options.why: Negating the time puts the latest order first on a tie.
Without negating the price, the lowest bid comes out first.
Time first gives the oldest bid, whatever its price.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. The highest price first, then the earliest time.

explain.text: The heap compares the first item, then the second on a tie. Negating the price makes the highest bid smallest; the plain time keeps earliest first.

quiz.prose: A sell at £100.02 is resting. A buy at £100.05 arrives and crosses it.
quiz.question: At what price do they trade?

options.why: That is the buyer's limit, the most it would pay. The resting order sets the price.
Fills are not split down the middle. The resting order's price stands.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Which order was in the book first?

explain.text: The resting sell offered £100.02, and the buyer accepted that offer. The buyer pays £0.03 less than its limit, a price improvement.

quiz.prose: 1,000 cancelled bids sit at the top of the bid heap. The next `best_bid()` pops all of them before it answers.
quiz.question: Is `best_bid` still cheap over a day?

options.text: Yes: each dead entry is popped once, so the work averages out
No: that call cost 1,000 pops, so every call costs that
options.why: Those entries are gone after this call. The next read starts from a clean top.

options.text: No: lazy deletion makes the heap grow without limit
options.why: Dead entries leave as soon as they reach the top, and each was pushed once.
